name: Vietnamese ca trù
lineage: Vietnamese ca trù chamber-vocal tradition of northern Vietnam. The form crystallized in the fifteenth century in Hanoi guild-house culture and developed through the late-imperial Lê and Nguyễn dynasties as the canonical literary-chamber form for the male literati class. Performance configuration: a female singer (ả đào) accompanies herself on the phách bamboo clapper (struck with a hardwood stick to mark cadence), with a male instrumentalist on đàn đáy (three-string long-necked fretted lute with unusually high frets enabling string-bending ornament) and a male patron-listener on the trống chầu praise-drum (struck to signal critical acclaim during performance — the patron is structurally part of the ensemble through this critical-response convention). The repertoire comprises forty-six canonical "thể-types" (poetic-meter categories) including hát nói (sung-recitation), múa bài bông (flower-offering dance accompaniment), hát giai (banquet song), and others — each thể with characteristic rhythmic-and-melodic conventions. Lyric base draws on classical Sino-Vietnamese poetic-meter forms. The mid-twentieth-century revolutionary-period cultural-policy suppressed ca trù as feudal, leading to near-extinction; the post-1990 revival under the guild-house Câu Lạc Bộ Ca Trù Hà Nội (Hanoi Ca Trù Club) and master-singer Quách Thị Hồ (1909-2001) restored continuity. Distinguished from southern Vietnamese hát ả đào by northern-dialect-specific cadential conventions; distinguished from chèo folk-opera by ca trù's solo-singer-with-chamber-trio (vs ensemble-theatrical) configuration; distinguished from quan họ by literary-chamber (vs village-festival-call-and-response) functional context.
